executive_summary: Spin bowling is a deception skill built around repeatable release, control of spin axis and revolutions, pace and flight changes, use of crease, field-setting pressure, and reading batter intent. The backend should not treat all spinners as one role: finger spin, wrist spin, left-arm orthodox, and left-arm wrist spin have different release mechanics, accuracy profiles, variation menus, physical demands, and injury risks. Spin plans should connect technical development with tactical context: pitch wear, rough, ball age, batter handedness, match format, scoring pressure, and field protection. S&C support should emphasize shoulder and hip rotational capacity, trunk control, forearm/wrist/finger capacity, repeated low-to-moderate intensity bowling volume, and safe workload progression rather than fast-bowler sprint/run-up loading.

key_concepts.concept: Spin bowlers should be classified by delivery mechanism and bowling arm, not only by the direction the ball turns.
key_concepts.details: Useful app families are off spin, leg spin, left-arm orthodox, and left-arm wrist spin. Each family needs different grip, release, stock-ball, variation, field, and matchup logic.

key_concepts.concept: A spinner's stock ball is the foundation of selection, fields, and variations.
key_concepts.details: Variation volume should not outrun stock-ball control. The backend should prioritize a repeatable stock ball before recommending high-risk variations.

key_concepts.concept: Spin axis changes how the ball drifts, dips, bounces, or turns.
key_concepts.details: Side spin tends to create lateral turn and drift, top spin can add dip and bounce, and backspin/underspin can alter skid or hold-up. Training should include axis awareness, not just 'turn it more'.

key_concepts.concept: Flight is controlled trajectory and pace deception, not simply bowling slower.
key_concepts.details: A useful flighted delivery challenges the batter's judgment of length and scoring risk while still landing on a threatening line.

key_concepts.concept: Pace variation is most valuable when the action stays similar.
key_concepts.details: If the arm speed, run-up rhythm, or body language changes obviously, better batters can read the variation early.

key_concepts.concept: Over/around the wicket and width on the crease change release angle, batter sightline, and attacking channel.
key_concepts.details: Crease use should be connected to batter handedness, field, rough, and desired dismissal mode.

key_concepts.concept: A worn or abrasive pitch can make spin more threatening through turn, variable bounce, or rough outside the batter's line.
key_concepts.details: The backend should adjust spin strategy when pitch wear and rough are present instead of giving a generic line-length plan.

key_concepts.concept: Spin tactics change sharply between red-ball control, ODI middle-over squeeze, and T20 wicket/risk management.
key_concepts.details: The same bowler may need patient attacking fields in red-ball cricket, defensive boundary protection in T20, and matchup-based plans in white-ball middle overs.

key_concepts.concept: Batter handedness changes the value of lines, angles, and variation risk.
key_concepts.details: Off spin to a right-hander, off spin to a left-hander, leg spin to a right-hander, and left-arm orthodox to a right-hander all need different default plans.

key_concepts.concept: Spin bowling usually has lower run-up and impact than pace bowling, but still creates repetitive shoulder, trunk, wrist, and finger load.
key_concepts.details: The backend should track overs, high-intensity net sessions, and variation practice volume for spinners rather than assuming they are low-risk because they bowl slower.

technical_models.model: Approach, gather, front-foot contact, trunk rotation, arm path, wrist/finger action, release, follow-through.
technical_models.coaching_use: Tag spin issues by phase so the app does not prescribe grip changes when the real issue is alignment, balance, or release timing.

technical_models.model: Finger spin creates revolutions primarily through forearm/wrist/finger action at the end of a sequential lower-body-to-trunk-to-arm chain.
technical_models.coaching_use: Train posture, front-side control, pelvis/shoulder rotation, and forearm pronation before asking the bowler to force the ball with the hand only.

technical_models.model: Wrist spin uses wrist position, shoulder path, and finger release to create a stock leg-break or left-arm wrist spin with variation potential.
technical_models.coaching_use: Protect control and action repeatability before adding googly, slider, flipper, or top-spinner volume.

technical_models.model: Line, length, spin rate, spin axis, pace, and release height must be stable enough that field plans make sense.
technical_models.coaching_use: Use target zones and outcome tracking before expanding variation menus.

technical_models.model: Air deviation, vertical drop, and post-bounce deviation are separate outcomes influenced by spin axis, spin rate, speed, seam angle, release height, and pitch interaction.
technical_models.coaching_use: Build drills that distinguish beating the batter in the air from beating the batter off the surface.

technical_models.model: The spinner varies trajectory and ball speed while preserving enough action similarity to delay batter recognition.
technical_models.coaching_use: Use constraints such as same arm speed or same run-up rhythm while changing release and trajectory.

technical_models.model: Changing position on the crease changes the visual angle and can bring stumps, pad, edge, or rough into play.
technical_models.coaching_use: Pair crease position with a named dismissal plan rather than using it randomly.

technical_models.model: Stock ball first, then top-spin or arm-ball style changes, then more deceptive or higher-risk variations.
technical_models.coaching_use: Keep beginner and intermediate spin plans focused on control and one safe variation before advanced deception skills.

technical_models.model: Spin bowling must preserve a fair delivery action; wrist flexion/rotation is allowed, but illegal elbow straightening after shoulder height is not.
technical_models.coaching_use: Flag legality-risk notes when users describe throwing, chucking, or painful elbow snap cues.

technical_models.model: Spin performance depends on controlled rotational mobility, trunk stiffness, shoulder external rotation tolerance, forearm/wrist/finger capacity, and repeatable balance.
technical_models.coaching_use: Connect gym work to spin outcomes: release repeatability, spin generation, shoulder durability, and bowling volume tolerance.

tactical_rules.rule: Build pressure around off stump and the outside edge with a field that rewards beating the outside edge or forcing a risky drive.
tactical_rules.application: Use slip/catcher when attacking, protect easy singles only after the batter has release options.

tactical_rules.rule: Use over/around wicket and rough options to bring bowled, lbw, bat-pad, and miscued drive into play.
tactical_rules.application: The best line depends on rough, batter sweep ability, and whether the ball is turning into or away from the scoring arc.

tactical_rules.rule: Threaten outside off with turn away while using top-spin or straighter variation to challenge the batter's length judgment.
tactical_rules.application: Do not overuse the googly before stock-ball control is stable.

tactical_rules.rule: Use angle across and spin away to challenge edge and drive control; use arm ball or straighter ball sparingly as a wicket threat.
tactical_rules.application: Crease width can create a stronger lbw/bowled threat if the batter plays across the line.

tactical_rules.rule: When rough is available outside the batter's line, prioritize repeatable landing areas over excessive variation.
tactical_rules.application: Variation is secondary; hitting the rough repeatedly increases uncertainty in bounce and deviation.

tactical_rules.rule: On flatter surfaces, create pressure through pace changes, angle, field protection, and forcing the batter to hit against the spin.
tactical_rules.application: Avoid assuming big turn; use drift, dip, stumps, and boundary dimensions.

tactical_rules.rule: When the ball is wet or hard to grip, reduce reliance on extreme revolutions and high-risk variations.
tactical_rules.application: Prioritize stable seam grip, stump-to-stump lines, defensive fields, and lower error plans.

tactical_rules.rule: Know the protected boundary and make the batter hit the lower-probability option.
tactical_rules.application: Field setting and bowling plan must be coupled; a good ball to one field can be a bad ball to another.

tactical_rules.rule: Sustain an attacking area long enough to build false-shot pressure rather than changing plan after every defended ball.
tactical_rules.application: Use close catchers when conditions and match state allow pressure.

tactical_rules.rule: Make the new batter play early with the stock ball before showing the full variation menu.
tactical_rules.application: Use fielders and line to test footwork, sweep judgment, and ability to rotate strike.

tactical_rules.rule: Adjust length, pace, and line instead of only moving fielders.
tactical_rules.application: Options include faster into the pitch, wider outside off, fuller to challenge lbw/bowled, or top-spin bounce depending on format and field.

tactical_rules.rule: Pre-plan line and field transitions for handedness changes to avoid rushed field moves and poor first-ball plans.
tactical_rules.application: Store separate default plans for each batter hand and spinner type.

physical_demands.demand: Repeated overarm bowling requires shoulder rotational range and tissue tolerance.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Spin bowlers may show substantial dominant-side rotational adaptation and need shoulder monitoring.

physical_demands.demand: Controlled pelvis and shoulder sequencing helps generate spin without forcing the wrist alone.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Finger-spin research links pelvis orientation and pelvis-shoulder separation with higher spin-rate outcomes.

physical_demands.demand: Spinners need controlled trunk rotation and anti-rotation to repeat release and manage cumulative load.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Supports release consistency and reduces compensation through shoulder or lower back.

physical_demands.demand: Grip endurance and finger/wrist capacity support repeated spin generation and variation practice.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Especially important for finger spinners and wrist spinners practicing high-repetition release drills.

physical_demands.demand: Front-foot contact and follow-through require repeatable balance.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Poor balance can change release point, line, and length.

physical_demands.demand: Long spells require repeatable concentration and physical rhythm.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Supports accuracy over spells without turning spin training into high-fatigue conditioning.

physical_demands.demand: Spinners need hip, thoracic, shoulder, wrist, and ankle mobility but also enough stiffness to control release.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: Excessive loose mobility without strength can reduce repeatability.

physical_demands.demand: Most spinners need acceleration and fielding athleticism, but less run-up intensity than fast bowlers.
physical_demands.spin_relevance: S&C should still develop fielding speed and repeated efforts without treating the spinner as a pace bowler.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repetitive overarm bowling can create shoulder overload, particularly when variation volume is high or range deficits are unmanaged.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Monitor bowling overs, add rotator cuff and scapular capacity, and avoid heavy overhead gym fatigue near high bowling volume.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: High repetition of wrist-spin, finger-spin, or new variations can irritate wrist, finger, or forearm structures.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Introduce variations in small blocks and track soreness after net sessions.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Repeated trunk rotation and poor alignment can provoke lower-back symptoms even when the bowler is not fast.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Use trunk-control training, hip mobility, and workload monitoring; avoid heavy axial loading immediately after long bowling spells.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Trying to force extra spin by snapping or straightening the elbow can create pain and legality concerns.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Cue wrist/finger/forearm action with a legal arm path and refer technical/legal concerns to a qualified cricket coach.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: A sudden jump in googly, doosra, flipper, carrom-ball, or high-force variation practice can overload small joints.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Cap new variation reps and preserve stock-ball volume as the main training exposure.

injury_or_load_risks.risk: Spinners also field and throw; shoulder load may come from bowling plus throws plus gym pressing.
injury_or_load_risks.mitigation: Treat total cricket arm load as bowling plus throwing plus overhead gym volume.

training_implications.implication: Do not apply fast-bowler workload and run-up stress rules directly to spin bowlers.
training_implications.application: Use lower impact running volume but stronger shoulder, trunk, wrist, and release-repeatability support.

training_implications.implication: Beginners and intermediates need control before a large variation library.
training_implications.application: Backend should restrict variation prompts by experience and stock-ball accuracy.

training_implications.implication: A red-ball spinner needs patience, repeatable attacking areas, and long-spell capacity; a T20 spinner needs matchup and boundary-management plans.
training_implications.application: Macro plan should use format as a condition for spin skill priorities.

training_implications.implication: Pitch wear, bounce, and rough should influence net targets and tactical rules.
training_implications.application: If rough is expected, practice repeated landing areas; if flat, practice pace/flight and scoring-denial plans.

training_implications.implication: Spinners are not exempt from shoulder monitoring.
training_implications.application: Daily snapshots should ask about shoulder, elbow, wrist, and finger symptoms after high-volume bowling.

training_implications.implication: Rotational power work is useful only if it supports repeatable release rather than uncontrolled effort.
training_implications.application: Use medicine ball throws, cable rotations, anti-rotation, and hip/trunk sequencing with low-to-moderate fatigue.

training_implications.implication: Advanced spin variations should unlock through control and workload tolerance, not just user interest.
training_implications.application: Require stable stock-ball accuracy, no wrist/finger pain trend, and coaching context before recommending high-risk variations.

training_implications.implication: A long spin net session is a real training load even if it does not feel as intense as pace bowling.
training_implications.application: Athlete_state should store balls/overs bowled, variation reps, perceived shoulder/wrist load, and next-day soreness.

backend_records_to_create.summary: Role profile for spin bowlers with sub-roles by spin family, match format, and tactical use.
Phase model for approach, gather, contact, rotation, release, and follow-through.
Model linking release, spin axis, spin rate, drift, dip, bounce, and turn.
Default line, field, and variation logic by spinner type and batter handedness.
Rules for rough, flat pitches, bounce, dew, wet ball, and worn red-ball conditions.
Tracks overs, variation reps, shoulder/wrist/finger symptoms, and throwing load.
S&C profile emphasizing shoulder, trunk, hip, wrist/finger capacity, balance, and spell repeatability.
Controls when advanced spin variations become available based on stock-ball control and pain/load status.
Stores balls bowled, spin family practiced, variation count, accuracy rating, and pain/readiness notes.

open_questions.question: Can the app infer spin axis or spin quality without video/computer vision?
open_questions.reason: User self-report is likely too vague for precise technical coaching.

open_questions.question: How should the app safely flag potential illegal action concerns without overstepping into umpiring or biomechanical diagnosis?
open_questions.reason: Bowling legality is technical and should be handled carefully.

open_questions.question: What youth spin-bowling workload caps are credible across countries?
open_questions.reason: Most public workload guidance is stronger for pace bowling than spin bowling.

open_questions.question: How much sport-science evidence exists specifically for left-arm wrist spin?
open_questions.reason: Most evidence and coaching material groups wrist spin together.

open_questions.question: How should the app adapt spin fields for local league rules, boundary sizes, and player skill level?
open_questions.reason: Tactical recommendations need format and fielding-quality context.
